items.stem: A stationary process is ergodic for the mean if:
options: its mean is constant over time
the sample mean converges in probability to the process mean
items.explanation: Equivalently, since the sample mean is unbiased, if Var(ȳₙ) → 0. Option B is part of stationarity, which does NOT imply ergodicity — the two are separate properties, and yₜ = Z + εₜ satisfies the first without the second.

items.stem: Does weak stationarity imply ergodicity?
options: Only if the mean is zero
items.explanation: The standard counterexample is yₜ = Z + εₜ with Z drawn once per realisation: it is stationary with mean 0, variance 2 and γₖ = 1 at every lag, yet its sample mean converges to Z rather than to 0. Stationarity concerns the ensemble at each time; ergodicity bridges ensemble and time averages.

items.stem: A sufficient condition for a stationary process to be ergodic for the mean is:
items.explanation: If the autocovariances decay, distant stretches of one realisation are nearly independent and act as separate samples, so Var(ȳₙ) → 0. The sharper sufficient condition Σ|γₖ| < ∞ additionally delivers the asymptotic variance. Note it is sufficient, not necessary.

items.stem: The variance of the sample mean of a stationary series equals:
items.explanation: The (1 − k/n) factor is the proportion of pairs available at lag k: there are n − k ordered pairs at that lag out of n possible. With independence every ρₖ is zero and the bracket reduces to 1, giving the familiar γ₀/n.
items.check: At n = 1 the formula must give γ₀, the variance of a single observation, which it does since the sum is empty.

items.stem: The long-run variance of an AR(1) with coefficient φ and shock variance σ² is:
items.explanation: It is γ₀(1 + φ)/(1 − φ), and since γ₀ = σ²/(1 − φ²) = σ²/((1−φ)(1+φ)) this reduces to σ²/(1 − φ)². At φ = 0.8 with σ² = 1 it is 25. Note option A is γ₀ itself, not the long-run variance.
items.check: At φ = 0 the two must coincide at σ², since the process is then white noise — and both formulas give σ².

items.stem: In the process yₜ = Z + εₜ with Z drawn once per realisation, the sample mean converges to:
options: Z, the value drawn for that realisation
items.explanation: ȳₙ = Z + ε̄ₙ, and ε̄ₙ → 0, so ȳₙ → Z. The realisation never forgets Z, so there is only ever one piece of information about the level however long the series runs. Simulated Var(ȳₙ) stayed at about 1 from n = 100 through n = 10,000.

items.stem: For an AR(1) with φ = 0.8, σ² = 1 and n = 200, the asymptotic variance of the sample mean is:
items.explanation: Long-run variance σ²/(1−φ)² = 1/0.04 = 25, so Var(ȳₙ) ≈ 25/200 = 0.125. The exact value is 0.122222 and the simulated 0.121690. Option B is γ₀/n = 2.7778/200, the value independence would give — nine times too small.
items.check: The exact figure must be slightly below the asymptotic one, since the (1 − k/n) weights discount the higher lags, and 0.1222 < 0.1250 ✓.

items.stem: The effective sample size of an AR(1) series of n observations is approximately:
items.explanation: At n = 200 this is 66.7 at φ = 0.5, 22.2 at φ = 0.8 and 10.5 at φ = 0.9. The formula is asymptotic: the exact figures at n = 200 are 11.0 at φ = 0.9 and 5.7 at φ = 0.95, so it is a guide rather than a precise count.
items.check: Positive autocorrelation must REDUCE the effective sample size, so the factor has to be below 1 for φ > 0 — which rules out option A at once.

items.stem: In the process yₜ = Z + εₜ with Z and εₜ independent standard normals, Z drawn once per realisation, the autocovariance at lag k ≥ 1 is:
items.explanation: Cov(Z + εₜ, Z + εₜ₋ₖ) = Var(Z) = 1, since the ε terms are independent of each other and of Z. The variance is γ₀ = 1 + 1 = 2, so ρₖ = 1/2 at every lag — never decaying, which is why the process is not ergodic. Option A is the autoCORRELATION, not the autocovariance.

items.stem: For an AR(1) with φ = −0.8, the variance of the sample mean compared with γ₀/n is:
options: smaller — the effective sample size is 9n
items.explanation: The factor is (1 + φ)/(1 − φ) = 0.2/1.8 = 1/9, so the variance is a NINTH of the independence value and n_eff = 9n. Consecutive observations are strongly negatively correlated, so they offset each other and their average is less variable than a single observation. Only positive autocorrelation costs information.

items.stem: Consider ergodicity and its consequences.
items.explanation: A is true — the counterexample establishes it. B is true: a finite MA has γₖ exactly zero beyond lag q. C is true, and it is the key practical distinction. D is false — negative autocorrelation improves precision, giving n_eff = 9n at φ = −0.8.
statements: A stationary process need not be ergodic.
A finite-order MA process is always ergodic for the mean.
Non-ergodicity makes the sample mean inconsistent, not merely imprecise.
Any autocorrelation, of either sign, reduces the precision of the sample mean.

A.why: True. yₜ = Z + εₜ with Z fixed per realisation is stationary with γ₀ = 2 and γₖ = 1 at every lag, yet Var(ȳₙ) → Var(Z) = 1 rather than 0.

B.why: True: γₖ is exactly zero beyond lag q, so the sufficient condition γₖ → 0 holds trivially. The MA(1) long-run variance is σ²(1 − θ)².

C.why: True, and it is why no standard-error correction helps: the sample mean converges to μ + Z rather than μ, and scaling a standard error cannot repair a point estimate that converges to the wrong value.

D.why: False. Negative autocorrelation IMPROVES precision — the factor (1+φ)/(1−φ) is 1/9 at φ = −0.8, so n_eff = 9n. Consecutive observations offset each other, which is more informative than independence.

items.stem: For an AR(1) with φ = 0.95, by what factor should a naive standard error σ̂/√n be multiplied?
items.explanation: The variance correction relative to γ₀/n is (1 + φ)/(1 − φ) = 1.95/0.05 = 39, so the STANDARD ERROR correction is √39 = 6.245. Option A is the variance factor, not the standard-error factor — confusing the two is the natural error here.
items.check: A standard-error multiplier must be the square root of a variance multiplier, so it has to be the smaller of the two candidates.

items.stem: An analyst has 50,000 readings from a single instrument with a fixed unknown calibration offset. To estimate the underlying quantity more precisely, the best route is:
options: more readings from the same instrument
a longer moving average of the existing readings
items.explanation: The readings are μ + Z + εₜ with Z the instrument's offset, so the sample mean converges to μ + Z and the residual error Var(Z) does not shrink with n. Averaging cannot touch a component present identically in every observation. Reducing it requires sampling the ENSEMBLE — more instruments — which is exactly why panel data combines a cross-section with a time dimension.

items.stem: Can ergodicity be established from a finite sample?
options: Yes, by testing whether the autocorrelations are zero
No — it is an asymptotic property, and near-unit-root ergodic data look like non-ergodic data
Yes, provided the sample exceeds 1,000 observations
items.explanation: At φ = 0.99 the autocorrelations look flat over twenty lags although they do eventually reach zero — ρ₅₀₀ = 0.0066 — whereas the non-ergodic example's ρₖ = 1/2 never moves. No finite window distinguishes them. A sample can raise suspicion, but the judgement rests on the mechanism: is there a fixed component attached to this realisation?

items.stem: For an MA(1) with yₜ = εₜ − θεₜ₋₁ and θ = 0.5, the long-run variance is:
items.explanation: γ₀ = σ²(1 + θ²) = 1.25σ² and γ₁ = −θσ² = −0.5σ², so the long-run variance is γ₀ + 2γ₁ = 1.25σ² − σ² = 0.25σ² = σ²(1 − θ)². The negative γ₁ reduces it well below γ₀, so the mean is estimated more precisely than independence would allow.
items.check: Option A is γ₀ itself, which would be the answer only if γ₁ were zero.

items.stem: Is a random walk ergodic for the mean?
options: Yes, since its increments are independent
No, because its autocorrelations do not decay
The question does not arise — a random walk is not stationary
items.explanation: Ergodicity is defined for stationary processes. A random walk has Var(yₜ) = tσ², growing without bound, so there is no constant mean for a sample mean to converge to — topic 7.6 shows its sample mean does not settle at all. Option C gives a reason that sounds right but applies to a stationary non-ergodic process, not to a non-stationary one.

items.stem: Consider the variance-of-the-mean formula in detail.
items.explanation: A is true — n − k ordered pairs out of n at each lag. B is true and is the finite-sample discount. C is true, and it is the algebraic signature of non-ergodicity. D is false: ergodicity for second moments is a separate and stronger requirement.
statements: The (1 − k/n) weight is the proportion of observation pairs available at lag k.
For a positively autocorrelated process the exact variance is below the asymptotic one.
In the non-ergodic counterexample the bracket grows like n, cancelling the 1/n.
Ergodicity for the mean implies ergodicity for second moments.

A.why: True. The double sum has n − k ordered pairs with i − j = k and the same with j − i = k, out of n² terms in all, which collects to the (1 − k/n) factor.

B.why: True — the weights discount the higher lags that the asymptotic sum counts in full. At φ = 0.9 the gap is 19% at n = 50 (1.623 against 2.000) but only 5% at n = 200 (0.4763 against 0.5000).

C.why: True. With ρₖ = 1/2 at every lag the bracket is approximately n − 1, so Var(ȳₙ) ≈ (γ₀/n)(n − 1) tends to a positive constant — exactly 1 + 1/n with γ₀ = 2, matching the direct calculation.

D.why: False — they are separate, and the second needs conditions on fourth moments. For a Gaussian stationary process γₖ → 0 delivers both, which is why the distinction rarely surfaces, but it is a genuine one.

items.stem: For an AR(1) with φ = 0.9, σ² = 1 and n = 50, the exact variance of the sample mean is 1.623 while the asymptotic formula gives 2.000. The 19% gap arises because:
options: the (1 − k/n) weights discount the long lags, which carry much of the long-run variance
the process is not ergodic at n = 50
items.explanation: When ρₖ = 0.9ᵏ decays slowly, a large share of Σγₖ sits at lags that the exact formula discounts by (1 − k/50) and the asymptotic sum counts in full. The gap shrinks to 5% at n = 200, so the asymptotic approximation needs a reasonably long series when persistence is high. Simulation gave 1.636, confirming the exact value.
items.check: The exact value must be the smaller of the two for a positively autocorrelated process, since every weight is at most 1.

items.stem: A series is persistent and ergodic. A colleague suggests a Newey–West long-run variance estimator; another says the data may have a fixed individual effect. Which concern must be resolved first?
options: the long-run variance, since it is estimable from the data
the individual effect — a long-run variance estimator returns a plausible number either way
neither, since both corrections can be applied together
whichever gives the smaller standard error
items.explanation: The two problems differ in kind. A persistent ergodic series has a consistent sample mean and merely an understated standard error, which the estimator corrects. A non-ergodic series has an INCONSISTENT sample mean, and no scaling of a standard error repairs a point estimate converging to the wrong value — yet the estimator will still return a number, wrong in a way the data do not reveal. So ergodicity has to be settled first, by thinking about where the data came from.

items.stem: Why is ergodicity listed as a syllabus topic in its own right rather than mentioned in passing?
options: because it is difficult to compute
because it is needed only for Gaussian processes
because it is the assumption on which identification, estimation and forecasting all rest
items.explanation: A sample ACF compared with a theoretical one, Yule–Walker estimates substituted from sample autocorrelations, a periodogram read as a spectral density — each takes a time average from one realisation as standing in for an ensemble expectation, and each is justified by ergodicity rather than by stationarity. Teaching estimation without it would be teaching a method with no justification.
